text: So far in this course, GPU memory has come up as a single-device constraint. In distributed training, it's the reason you need more than one device in the first place. This lesson covers the two separate pressures — memory and time — that push a training job from one GPU to many.

It's tempting to size GPU memory off parameter count alone. A seven-billion-parameter model in FP16 is only about fourteen gigabytes — well under an eighty-gigabyte GPU. That estimate misses almost everything. Training keeps gradients, one per parameter, the same size as the weights again. It keeps optimizer state — Adam's first and second moment estimates per parameter, usually in FP32 for stability — which alone can run roughly four times the size of the parameters. And it keeps activations, the intermediate outputs saved for the backward pass, which scale with batch size and sequence length rather than model size.

Add it up for that same seven-billion-parameter model: fourteen gigabytes of parameters, fourteen of gradients, and around fifty-six of optimizer state. That's already past eighty gigabytes before a single activation is stored. The optimizer state, not the weights, is usually what breaks the budget first — a model doesn't need to be frontier-scale to outgrow one GPU.

Now suppose a model genuinely does fit, memory and all. Training can still be impractical on one GPU, because total training compute scales with both model size and dataset size. Frontier models train on trillions of tokens, and even a GPU capable of hundreds of teraflops would take months to grind through that alone — where the business need is days.

That's the second, independent pressure: even when memory isn't the limiter, wall-clock time is. These two problems call for two different fixes, which the next lesson breaks down in detail. When the model fits but training takes too long, the answer is data parallelism — replicate the model, split the dataset. When the model itself doesn't fit, replication never even gets off the ground — the answer is model parallelism, splitting the model itself across GPUs. Production clusters often need both at once.
